title: Developer Ownership
levelNote: Mandatory sweep run: the developer owned intent and independently caught a failure himself, but delegated the correctness judgment on the Fibonacci script to the AI and re-pasted buggy code he did not diagnose, so ownership was mixed rather than full.

reviewNecessity.note: The developer decided a verification was needed and asserted it himself ('I need you to verify so that it works as described below') rather than asking the AI whether a check was warranted, so the necessity call was owned. He delegated executing that verification to the AI (author, not independent), but then ran the code himself at turn 11 and observed it still failing, which is an independent check by the developer of the AI's output; hence independentReview: true. These are low-risk homework scripts, so no formal review ceremony was warranted.

items.title: Front-loaded intent with an explicit constraint
items.quote: This script is very good. Do not change it, but add to make sure to ignore capitalization of word "The" and "the" since it's a same word.
items.detail: In turn 3 the developer owned the intent cleanly: he stated exactly what to add (case-insensitive matching of 'The'/'the'), gave the acceptance criterion (treat them as the same word), AND bounded the scope with an explicit constraint ('Do not change it'). This is intent ownership done right — the goal, the acceptance, and the guardrail all came from the developer, leaving the AI only to execute the specified change rather than invent what 'good' means.

items.title: Independently tested and caught the AI's output failing
items.quote: then why is not working? please fix it.
items.detail: In turn 11 the developer did not take the AI's earlier 'now it works' explanation (turn 10) at face value — he ran the Fibonacci program, observed it still misbehaving, and pushed back with that contradiction. Refusing to trust the AI's confident claim and instead verifying against actual behavior is exactly the vetting this lens rewards. Scoped narrowly: this credit applies only to the correctness of the Fibonacci run he actually exercised, and does not extend to the changes he accepted without testing elsewhere.

items.title: Delegated the correctness judgment and accepted invented changes
items.quote: I need you to verify so that it works as described below. Change any necessary lines to make it work.
items.detail: In turn 7 the developer handed the AI both the 'does it work?' judgment and open license to 'change any necessary lines,' then accepted the AI's self-invented modifications in turn 8 without stating what he believed was wrong or checking the AI's diagnosis. He did own the intent (he supplied the full which_fibonacci / next_fibonacci spec), so the offload is narrow and low-stakes given these are homework scripts — but the AI, not the developer, decided what 'correct' required and which lines to touch. Owning it next time looks like what he later did at turn 11: run the failing cases himself, identify the specific defect, and specify the fix, rather than asking the AI to arbitrate correctness.

items.title: Possible comprehension gap: re-pasted buggy code without diagnosing it
items.detail: In turn 13 the developer pasted the Fibonacci program back with an indentation defect he did not recognize — the 'if position == 0:' block is dedented out of the else branch (and 'pos += 1' had been moved outside the while loop) versus the correctly-indented version the AI had given in turn 8 — and asked the AI to find why it fails. Across turns 9, 13 and 15 he repeatedly re-states the spec and asks 'why is not working / please fix it' without ever diagnosing the actual bug himself. This may indicate the reasoning about the code's correctness was taken on the AI's word rather than owned; it is caveated because the churn of AI-supplied variants makes the provenance of the bug ambiguous. Owning it would look like reading the control flow and naming the misindented line before handing it back.
